title: Public health approaches: prevention and health promotion
subject: subj:pubhealth1

provenance.note: Public Health Approaches.pdf (Public Health, Pr. Safwane Mouwafaq)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Prevention: prevent onset, stop progression, reduce consequences (WHO 1984).
Primary: reduce incidence (vaccination, education, smoking cessation); most cost-effective.
Secondary: early detection (screening, TB skin test, contact tracing).
Tertiary: reduce disability and recurrence (rehab, palliation, surveillance).
Screening needs: frequent serious disease, effective treatment, feasible early mass diagnosis.
Health promotion: Ottawa 1986; enabling people to increase control over their health.
Prerequisites: peace, shelter, education, food, income, ecosystem, resources, justice, equity.
5 pillars: healthy public policy, supportive environments, community action, personal skills, reorient services.
Prevention: biomedical, vertical, population as object. Promotion: bio-psycho-social, horizontal, population as subject.

deeper.title: Why primary prevention is the most cost-effective
deeper.html:
Every case prevented saves the whole cost of diagnosis, treatment, disability and lost productivity, and a vaccine or a smoking-cessation programme reaches many people for little money. Secondary and tertiary prevention act after disease has started, so they reduce but cannot erase these costs.

Source: the lecture's primary prevention slide.

deeper.title: Why prevention alone is not enough
deeper.html:
Prevention programmes tell people what to do about specific risks, which works well for infections with a clear cause. Chronic diseases arise from many interacting determinants (income, education, environment), which directives alone cannot change. Health promotion adds policies, environments and community participation to act on those causes, which is why the lecture calls it the future of public health.

Source: the lecture's prevention vs promotion comparison.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Biostatistics: describe, compare and interpret health data.
Qualitative: nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered). Quantitative: discrete or continuous.
Sex = qualitative nominal; number of children = quantitative discrete.
Dependent variable = the outcome.
Cross-sectional (snapshot), cohort (exposure → outcome), case-control (diseased vs not).
Normal curve: symmetric, mean = median = mode.
Shapiro-Wilk: p > 0.05 → normal; p ≤ 0.05 → not normal.
Nominal → bar chart; continuous → histogram/box plot.
2 qualitative → chi-square (Fisher if small).
Qual + quant → t-test (normal) or Mann-Whitney.
2 quantitative → Pearson (normal) or Spearman.

deeper.title: Why normality decides the test
deeper.html:
The t-test and Pearson correlation rely on means and standard deviations, which describe data well only when the distribution is roughly symmetric. With skewed data or outliers, the mean is pulled away from most values, so rank-based tests (Mann-Whitney, Spearman) that use order rather than size give more reliable answers. That is why the Shapiro-Wilk check comes before choosing a test.

Source: the study guide's decision tree.

deeper.title: Why p > 0.05 does not prove normality
deeper.html:
The Shapiro-Wilk test starts from the hypothesis that the data are normal and looks for evidence against it. A p-value above 0.05 means there is not enough evidence to reject normality, which in practice lets us treat the data as normal; it is not proof, especially in small samples where tests have little power.

Source: the study guide's normality section.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Determinants: who they are, what they do, in which conditions.
Non-modifiable CVD factors: age, sex, family history, ethnicity.
Modifiable CVD factors: smoking, inactivity, diet, obesity, BP, LDL, diabetes, alcohol, stress.
Activity target: ≥ 150 min/week moderate-to-vigorous.
High BP: > 140/90 (130/80 with diabetes).
Protective factors shield; risk factors worsen.
Dever (1976): weighting determinants; risk of blaming individuals.
Social determinants (Marmot; WHO CSDH 2007): education, environment, community support.
Modifiable determinants guide public health interventions.

deeper.title: Why behaviours are not purely individual choices
deeper.html:
Smoking, diet and physical activity look like personal decisions, but they follow the conditions people live in: education, income, neighbourhood food shops, safe places to exercise, advertising and stress. Blaming individuals alone ignores these upstream causes, which is why the lecture asks whether responsibilising individuals is fair and turns to social determinants.

Source: the lecture's discussion of Dever's model and Marmot.

deeper.title: Why modifiable factors matter for prevention
deeper.html:
Age, sex and genes cannot be changed, but they identify who is at higher risk. Modifiable factors are where action is possible: stopping smoking, controlling blood pressure, moving more. Public health programmes combine both, targeting high-risk groups with changes in modifiable determinants.

Source: the lecture's synthesis slide.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Epidemiology: epi upon + demos people + logy science.
Last (1988): distribution and determinants of health-related states in populations, applied to prevention and control.
Distribution = time, place, person; determinants = factors influencing health.
Endemic (constant), epidemic (excess), pandemic (worldwide).
Hippocrates; Ibn al-Khatib (contagion); Graunt 1662 (mortality data); Lind 1747 (first controlled trial, scurvy); Farr (vital statistics); Snow (cholera); Doll and Hill (smoking).
Descriptive → hypotheses; analytical → test hypotheses.
Observational: descriptive, case-control, cohort. Experimental: RCT, field, community trials.
Evidence pyramid: systematic reviews at the top.

deeper.title: Why comparison is the heart of epidemiology
deeper.html:
A single observation, such as lung cancer in a smoker, proves nothing: the key is whether the disease is more frequent among smokers than non-smokers. Epidemiology gets its power from comparing groups (exposed vs unexposed, cases vs controls), which is what turns observations into evidence about causes.

Source: the lecture's approach of an epidemiologist.

deeper.title: Why randomisation sits high on the pyramid
deeper.html:
In observational studies, people who choose an exposure may differ in many other ways, which can distort results. Randomly assigning the intervention balances those hidden differences between groups, so a difference in outcomes can be attributed to the intervention. That is why RCTs, and reviews that combine them, provide the strongest evidence.

Source: the lecture's study designs and evidence pyramid.

labels: Descriptive: who, what, where, when → hypotheses
Evidence pyramid: systematic reviews on top, opinion at base

title: Health indicators and measures of disease frequency
subject: subj:pubhealth1

provenance.note: Health Indicators.pdf (Public Health, Pr Karima El Rhazi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Health indicator: quantitative measure of health status, trends or performance.
Domains: health status, risk factors, service coverage, health systems.
Proportion (prevalence), rate (incidence), ratio (a:b).
Prevalence = existing cases; point vs period (lifetime).
Incidence = new cases in the population at risk.
Cumulative incidence = risk (closed cohort); incidence rate = cases / person-time.
Rare disease (< 5%): incidence rate ≈ proportion.
Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration.
Crude mortality: all deaths / population; cause-specific: one cause.
Case fatality: deaths among cases, a measure of severity.

deeper.title: Why person-time is a better denominator
deeper.html:
In real studies people enter late, leave early, or develop the disease partway through. Counting each person's disease-free time (person-years) credits exactly how long they were at risk, so the incidence rate reflects the true speed of new cases. Cumulative incidence works only in a closed group followed for the same period.

Source: the lecture's incidence rate slides.

deeper.title: Why a chronic disease can have high prevalence with low incidence
deeper.html:
Diabetes or hypertension may have relatively few new cases each year, but patients live with them for decades, so cases accumulate like water in a bath with a small outflow. An acute infection with high incidence but short duration can have low prevalence at any given moment. This is why prevalence reflects the burden on services and incidence reflects risk.

Source: the lecture's incidence-prevalence relationship.

exam_points: WHO 1948: complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease.
Winslow: science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life, promoting health through organised efforts.
Clinical: sick individuals, at contact, doctor's power. Public health: whole population, lifelong, costs, participation.
Holistic care: physical, psychological, social, multidisciplinary.
Prevention acts before disease; promotion empowers and builds supportive environments.
CVD: leading cause of death (> 17 million/year, ~31%).
Chadwick 1842, Snow (cholera), Virchow (social factors), Pasteur and Koch (germ theory).
Public Health Act 1848 (UK).
NCDs ≈ 70% of global deaths.
Public health problem criteria: inequalities/vulnerability and social perception.

deeper.title: Why public health must consider costs
deeper.html:
A clinician treats the patient in front of them; a public health planner must decide how limited money is spread across a whole population. Screening everyone, building parks or running a vaccination campaign has to be weighed against other uses of the same budget, which is why the public health approach explicitly takes costs into account.

Source: the lecture's clinical vs public health approach table.

deeper.title: Why the ER case starts a public health course
deeper.html:
The boy's wound can be stitched in minutes, but his anxiety, homelessness and family conflict will decide his health in the months ahead. The case shows the three dimensions of the WHO definition (physical, mental, social) in one patient, and why doctors need public health thinking even in emergency medicine.

Source: the lecture's case study.
